newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Aussie dlr shies, rate cut talk turns to size.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Aussie dlr shies, rate cut talk turns to size.

text.p: The Australian dollar began to show the wear and tear of weeks of rate cut speculation on Friday as a dismal set of retail sales data suggested the real question was not if an easing would come, but how big it would be.
Sales seemed to have stepped off a cliff in September with a steep 3.7 percent fall. This was the biggest monthly drop since April 1994 and dwarfed market forecasts of a 0.5 percent dip.
"Given the recent weak data, there must now be a significant chance the rate cut will be 75 basis points rather than 50," said Chris Caton, chief economist at BT Australia.
By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the local currency had shrunk back to US$0.7896/01, its lowest close in three weeks, from an early US$0.7915/20 and US$0.7917/22 late here Thursday.
Traders said exporter bids were expected around US$0.7885 which should cushion the currency and there was talk that the rush of A$ samurai issues seen this week would continue next.

For today, however, the flow of issues seemed to have paused and Japanese investors were inclined to take profits, wearing the down to 89.70/80 yen fom an early 90.20/30 and Thursday's 90.08/18. That took its toll in trade weighted terms and the currency closed at 58.4 from a previous 58.6 finish.
The market had been discounting a 0.5 point cut in domestic interest rates to 6.5 percent for some weeks without scaring away offshore investors from the local dollar.
A steep fall in Q3 inflation had boosted the Reserve Bank's anti-inflation credibility and provided scope for policy to be eased while keeping real yield differentials attractive.
That attraction was clearly seen in the rush of A$-denominated dual currency samurai bonds this week, which had so far totalled around 135 billion yen or A$1.5 billion.
But analysts wondered if demand would last if rates were cut by more than 0.5 point, as today's retail sales shocker hinted.

The plunge in September more than wiped out gains of 1.1 and 1.0 percent in August and July respectively and real retail sales for the quarter managed only a meagre 0.6 percent rise against the 1.3 percent analysts had expected.
They estimated sales would now add only 0.1 point to expenditure based GDP for the quarter, against their original expectations of 0.3 to 0.4 point.

"The quarterly data point to something a little harder than a soft landing and suggest overall economic growth may be slipping to well below potential," warned Stephen Koukoulas, senior economist at Citibank Australia.
Koukoulas said the case for a rate cut at next week's RBA board meeting was now overwhelming and assessed the chance of an easing at a near-certain 80 percent.
The bank's policy board meets Tuesday and, since that is also a holiday in Melbourne, most analysts expect the bank to move on Wednesday morning.
If it remained silent, the market was likley to assume a cut had been postponed until wages data later in the month and the dollar was likely to rally while bonds and bills slipped.
Dealers reckoned the dollar could weather a 0.5 point cut, but felt any more than that would see it test US$0.7850 support.
Futures were already contemplating a larger cut -- the March 90-day bank bill future was implying a rate of 6.28 percent.

That was a dangerous scenario for the dollar since commodity prices were also under pressure. The influential Commodity Research Bureau index plunged 3.83 points Thursday to a 14-month low of 237.83. It was led by oil, grains and sugar, all of which are bif export earners for Australia.

"The AUD will walk a tightrope in coming weeks," said Hans Kunnen, chief economist at Colonial State Bank. "Commodity prices have crashed and the currency is substantially at risk of losing investors support." -- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
